title: Starting Point, End Point
subtitle: It's a law of physics. There are no exceptions.

items.text: Starting Point, End Point

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: So, then, their parents are the protesters we encountered at the march …

items.speaker: X
items.text: Yes. Their parents have been protesting outside Wilson Pharmaceuticals for days now. So I offered to watch their kids.

items.speaker: X
items.text: I wanted to give these kids a bit of a break—make something fun for them, you know?

items.speaker: X
items.text: A lot of them have been in and out of hospitals for a long time, so I thought they could use something to lift their spirits.

items.speaker: X
items.text: Hopefully, they'll never have to know why their parents were protesting.
So you decided to make a toy for them?
items.edge_label: 所以你给他们制作了玩具？

items.speaker: X
items.text: Oh, it wasn't just a toy.

items.speaker: X
items.text: I prefer to describe it as a project.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: It seems you're very passionate about this project.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Mr. X, it was very kind of you to create such an ... amusement for these children.
But there's another angle to it: You got them involved.

items.speaker: X
items.text: A sense of involvement is important for attracting an audience.
But your investors protested the product didn't meet expectations?
items.edge_label: 然后被投资人抗议产品不符预期？

items.speaker: X
items.text: Well, I can't help that. I can't just let little kids run around with a marble launcher that just shoots off anywhere, now can I?

items.speaker: X
items.text: Still, seems like I'm not so good at building a "respectable" rapport with these kids.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: You sell yourself short, Mr. X. It's plainly clear they like you.

items.speaker: X
items.text: Aha, well, I appreciate your confidence.

items.speaker: X
items.text: The way they play reminds me a lot of the other kids, who played in the orphanage growing up.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Orphanage …?

items.speaker: X
items.text: Yes, it's a bit different from growing up in the St. Pavlov Foundation, like you did.

items.speaker: X
items.text: Back then, I had lots of siblings. I would often make machines like this. I'd get them to invest too …

items.speaker: X
items.text: But later …

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Oh no, did something happen?

items.speaker: X
items.text: —I joined the Foundation, and well, frankly, it's hard to find the same sort of investors there.
Is that so?

items.speaker: X
items.text: Of course. My brothers and sisters back then would give me anything I needed, just to see what I'd make. But when it comes to convincing adults, like Laplace and Mesmer … They're not so eager, especially that overbearing complainer.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Hmm, what was that about Ms. Mesmer?

items.speaker: X
items.text: Oh. Nothing, nothing. She's a fine colleague.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Oh, perhaps I heard you wrong.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: But what Sophie just said does remind me of something Ms. Mesmer Jr. has said about mankind.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: "One only needs to press the button to activate the feature. The toggle switch connects the circuits …"

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: "If only the human condition could be repaired like a machine."

items.speaker: X
items.text: Ms. Sonetto … do you realize that's an excellent proposition on mechanical theory?

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: What do you mean? I'm afraid I don't know anything at all about mechanical theory ...

items.speaker: X
items.text: No, no. What you just quoted, or should I say, "proposed," is precisely what lies at the heart of the LSCC's ethos.

items.speaker: X
items.text: "If we know the state of the universe at some initial time, we can determine its state at any other time."

items.speaker: X
items.text: The ultimate goal of the LSCC is to build an omniscient, intelligent machine capable of doing just that.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Is that so ... That would be an amazing feat!

items.speaker: X
items.text: But I'm afraid this would still not achieve Ms. Mesmer's ideal.

items.speaker: X
items.text: Ms. Sonetto, if society were to behave like a perfect machine, and each element would follow a precise and predictable orbit. What would determine who benefits from the system and who doesn't?

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: The system …?

items.speaker: X
items.text: The initial point.

items.speaker: X
items.text: Because in a measured orbit, everything is predetermined. So we only need to calculate the initial position of any one part to calculate all its states from past to future in the orbit.

items.speaker: X
items.text: Therefore, if the ball is set to move from point A to point B, then it might be that wealth is destined to flow from the poor to the rich.

items.speaker: X
items.text: And because the system is so designed that only those who pay get treatment, so individuals with higher starting points will receive the greater benefits.

items.speaker: X
items.text: It's a rational system and a legal one, for now. No surprises and no miracles.
You seem to be confusing social systems for mechanistic ones.
items.edge_label: 你将社会制度和机械理论混为一谈

items.speaker: X
items.text: Fundamentally, there is no difference between humans and machines.

items.speaker: X
items.text: Oh, I apologize, I've gone off-topic … Ms. Sonetto, would you mind helping me clean this up?

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Happy to help!

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: But what did you mean by "the initial point?"
TO BE CONTINUED…
